title: How to Verify a Business Is Legitimate Before You Pay or Lend
summary: To verify a business is legitimate, stack evidence from state registration and good standing, EIN and licenses, contact details and domain age, sanctions screening, ownership, UCC liens, and business credit data. This guide gives US lenders and anyone vetting a company a 10-step method, red flags, and how to report a scam.
body_markdown:
To verify a business is legitimate, confirm its registration and good standing with the Secretary of State, then validate its EIN, identifiers, and licenses. Next, cross-check its address, phone number, email domain, and website, and screen it against sanctions lists, complaints, UCC liens, and business credit data. Finally, watch for red flags such as payment pressure or missing documents, because no single check proves a business is real.


This guide is written for US lenders, fintechs, and risk teams running know-your-business (KYB) checks, and it also helps anyone vetting a vendor. You will learn what each official source confirms, where each one stops, and how to turn the checks into a repeatable verification workflow.


### Know What a Legitimate Business Looks Like on Paper


A legitimate business is registered where it claims, holds the licenses its work requires, is run by identifiable people, and operates as described. Each official record confirms only one of those facts, so verification means stacking evidence until the picture is consistent.


The California Attorney General's[background-check guidance](https://www.oag.ca.gov/consumers/general/checking_business_bkgrd10) says there is "no one-stop shop for checking out companies or surefire way of avoiding scams." The page was last updated in 2019, but that core advice still holds.


Registry data has limits as well, because the state records what the entity filed without verifying who owns it or whether it operates.


### Reported Fraud Losses Reached Record Highs in 2025


**$15.9 billion** in fraud losses were reported to the FTC in 2025 across about 3 million reports, according to[FTC congressional testimony](https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/ftc-testimony-jec-hearing-on-the-rising-scam-economy.pdf) . That figure rose from the more than $12.5 billion consumers reported losing in 2024, per an[FTC release on 2024 fraud data](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/03/new-ftc-data-show-big-jump-reported-losses-fraud-125-billion-2024) .


The FBI's[2025 Internet Crime Report](https://www.ic3.gov/AnnualReport/Reports/2025_IC3Report.pdf) logged $20.877 billion in reported losses across 1,008,597 complaints, up 26% from $16.6 billion in 2024. Business email compromise (BEC) was the second-largest loss category at about $3.05 billion, and 86% of BEC transactions moved by wire or ACH.


The[FTC also reported](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/06/ftc-data-show-people-reported-losing-3-point-5-billion-imposter-scams-2025) $3.5 billion in imposter scam losses in 2025, including nearly $1 billion to business impersonators.


These numbers are self-reported and incomplete, and they measure losses by consumers and payers rather than fraud by business loan applicants. They still show why a few minutes of verification before money moves is worth the effort.


#### How Fake Companies Win Trust


Scammers borrow credibility from names people already recognize, and the[FTC found](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/06/ftc-data-show-people-reported-losing-3-point-5-billion-imposter-scams-2025) that bank impersonators drove the highest reported losses among business impersonators in 2025.


The[California AG warns](https://www.oag.ca.gov/consumers/general/checking_business_bkgrd10) that "it's pretty easy for a company to get a fake address, phone number, and website." The[IC3 report](https://www.ic3.gov/AnnualReport/Reports/2025_IC3Report.pdf) adds that businesses reported over $30 million in BEC losses involving AI.


Scammers also pose as government agencies, and[FinCEN warns](https://www.fincen.gov/boi) of ownership-reporting scams that use fake forms and invented agencies.

For lenders and embedded finance platforms, verification is one stage of the underwriting data workflow. Applicant details are checked against KYB, credit, and fraud data, and mismatches are flagged before a decision, as Lendflow's guide to[application processing software](https://www.lendflow.com/post/how-application-processing-software-helps-lenders-fund-faster) explains.

### How to Verify a Business Is Legitimate in 10 Steps


Work through these steps in order, and record the source, date, and result of each check. Earlier steps confirm the entity exists, while later steps test the people, money, and risk behind it.


#### Step 1: Confirm Registration and Good Standing With the Secretary of State


Search the business registry of the Secretary of State, or equivalent office, in the state where the business says it was formed. Use the exact legal name and entity number, and note the formation state and any states where it is registered to do business.


The[California Secretary of State](https://www.sos.ca.gov/business-programs/business-entities/information-requests) record shows the entity name, number, status, addresses, agent for service of process, and listed officers or managers. The same page says ownership, phone numbers, email addresses, and EINs are not part of the record, and the office does not issue business licenses.


Read every status line rather than stopping at "Active." California lists Franchise Tax Board standing as a separate field. Its Certificate of Status certifies current status, such as active, suspended, dissolved, or cancelled.


In Delaware, lenders should request a certificate of good standing rather than rely on an online status check. The Division of Corporations'[sample certificate page](https://corp.delaware.gov/sample-certificate-wording/) lists good-standing certificates as well as certificates for void, forfeited, and cancelled entities.


Two details help you avoid false alarms. First, the[SBA](https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/launch-your-business/register-your-business) says a sole proprietor operating under their own legal name may not register anywhere, so a missing record needs context.


Second, the registered agent address is where legal papers are delivered, and the SBA notes that many owners use a registered agent service. Oregon[requires a physical street address](https://sos.oregon.gov/business/pages/registered-agents-service-of-process.aspx) for the agent rather than a PO box or mail forwarder. Its Secretary of State also notes that people can be listed as agents without consent.


#### Step 2: Validate the EIN and Other Business Identifiers


Ask the business for its Employer Identification Number and supporting IRS documentation, because there is no public IRS lookup that we could confirm. The[IRS](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/employer-identification-number) confirms an EIN only to people authorized for the entity, through an entity transcript, a CP 575 notice, or Letter 147C.


IRS[Publication 2108](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p2108.pdf) states that "IRS will not divulge an entity's name or TIN."[IRS TIN Matching](https://www.irs.gov/government-entities/indian-tribal-governments/taxpayer-identification-number-tin-on-line-matching) is limited to authorized payers filing certain information returns, so it is not a general KYB lookup.


The IRS also restricts how TIN Matching results may be used, as[Publication 2108](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p2108.pdf) explains, so teams should review IRS rules before relying on them. Lenders should collect the EIN document directly and compare the legal name on it with the state record.


Other identifiers carry less weight, and Dun & Bradstreet says a[D-U-N-S Number](https://www.dnb.com/en-us/smb/duns/what-is-a-duns-number.html) is free and not required to operate a business. Having one is weak evidence of legitimacy, and lacking one is not a warning sign.


For public companies and other SEC filers,[SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/search-filings) offers free access to filings by name, state, or SIC code. Most private businesses never file with the SEC, so absence from EDGAR proves nothing.


#### Step 3: Check Required Licenses and Registrations


Licenses depend on what a business does and where it operates, according to the[SBA](https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/launch-your-business/register-your-business) . The[California AG](https://www.oag.ca.gov/consumers/general/checking_business_bkgrd10) notes that contractors, doctors, lawyers, and brokers cannot do business without a valid license or registration.


Go to the state licensing board for the industry and compare the license holder, classification, and status with the business on the application. California's[Contractors State License Board](https://www.cslb.ca.gov/) licenses about 285,000 contractors in 45 classifications and offers a public License Check.


[FINRA BrokerCheck](https://www.finra.org/investors/investing/working-with-investment-professional/about-brokercheck) lets you research the backgrounds of brokers, brokerage firms, and investment adviser firms. Broker and firm records come from FINRA's registration database, while adviser data comes from the SEC.


[NMLS Consumer Access](https://mortgage.nationwidelicensingsystem.org/about/Documents/InformationAboutNMLSConsumerAccess.pdf) shows state-licensed companies, branches, and individuals in NMLS, mainly in mortgage, consumer finance, money services, and debt, according to[CSBS](https://www.csbs.org/nonbank-licensing-and-examination) . Pending applications do not appear, so use the tool that matches the business.


#### Step 4: Cross-Check the Address, Phone Number, and Email Domain


The FTC's[ReportFraud guidance](https://reportfraud.ftc.gov/faq/faq-topic/5) says "anyone can put up a website under almost any name." It advises confirming a company's physical address and phone number first. Find the contact details independently instead of relying only on what the business sent.


Map the operating address and confirm it is a real place of business that fits the company's size and industry. Keep in mind that a registered agent address shows where legal papers go, which may differ from where the business operates.


Call the main number from a public listing and confirm that someone answers in the company's name. Check that email comes from a domain the company controls and that the domain matches its website and legal name.


#### Step 5: Inspect the Website and Domain Age With RDAP


The[California AG](https://www.oag.ca.gov/consumers/general/checking_business_bkgrd10) suggests checking a website's registration data to see whether it "was created recently or will expire soon." A brand-new domain behind a company claiming years of history deserves a closer look.


Use the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) for this lookup. According to[ICANN](https://www.icann.org/en/contracted-parties/registry-operators/resources/registration-data-access-protocol) , RDAP was created to replace WHOIS, and since January 28, 2025, most generic top-level domains no longer have to offer WHOIS.


ICANN's[RDAP Lookup Tool](https://lookup.icann.org/) is a free client that runs RDAP queries from your browser, as ICANN[describes](https://www.icann.org/en/contracted-parties/registry-operators/registration-data-access-protocol/information-for-rdap-users-31-08-2018-en) . Treat a professional design as neutral, and look for named leaders, consistent branding, and contact details that match your other checks.


#### Step 6: Search Reviews and Complaints, and Read BBB Data With Care


Search the company name alongside "review," "complaint," and "scam," as the[FTC recommends](https://reportfraud.ftc.gov/faq/faq-topic/5) . Look for patterns across several sources rather than reacting to one angry post.


A low complaint count can mislead, and the[California AG](https://www.oag.ca.gov/consumers/general/checking_business_bkgrd10) advises readers not to "assume the company is legitimate just because it has few complaints." The office also says it cannot comment on whether a particular company is legitimate, and while some state AGs publish complaint information, many do not.


BBB data needs the same care, because BBB accreditation is a program businesses apply to join for a fee. It requires affirming BBB's eight[Standards for Trust](https://www.bbb.org/business/accreditation/standards) , roughly six months of selling or a similar prior business, and at least a B rating.


BBB says a rating is[its opinion](https://www.bbb.org/about/overview-of-ratings) of how a business is likely to interact with customers and "is not a guarantee" of reliability. For financial companies, the[CFPB stopped publishing](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/about-us/newsroom/the-cfpb-to-cease-discretionary-publication-of-complaint-narratives-and-visualizations/) complaint narratives on August 14, 2026, though structured complaint data is still published.


#### Step 7: Screen the Business and Its Owners Against OFAC Sanctions Lists


Run the business name and each owner through OFAC's[Sanctions List Search](https://sanctionssearch.ofac.treas.gov/) , which checks the SDN list and non-SDN lists. The tool uses approximate string matching, so similar names can return possible matches.


Review every possible match, including the program codes attached to each record. OFAC states that the tool "is not a substitute for undertaking appropriate due diligence," so a clean search is a first screen only.


#### Step 8: Identify and Verify Beneficial Owners


Find out who owns and controls the business, then verify those people's identities. Under FinCEN's[CDD Rule](https://www.fincen.gov/resources/statutes-and-regulations/cdd-rule-faqs) , covered financial institutions must verify each individual owning 25% or more, plus one person with significant control.


Covered institutions include federally regulated banks, federally insured credit unions, mutual funds, and securities broker-dealers. Whether a fintech or embedded lender is covered depends on its charter and bank partnerships, so teams should confirm their status with counsel. Other lenders can adopt the standard as good practice.


The rule lets institutions rely on ownership information the customer certifies, unless facts call its reliability into question. Since February 13, 2026, covered institutions may limit re-verification to the first account opening, new red flags, and their own risk-based triggers.


A federal ownership filing will not back this up for most applicants. As of August 2026, FinCEN's[final BOI rule](https://www.fincen.gov/boi) made the March 2025 exemption permanent, so US companies no longer file BOI reports. Foreign companies registered in a US state can still be reporting companies.


These rules may change, so collect ownership details directly from the applicant and verify the individuals behind them.


#### Step 9: Search UCC Filings for Liens


Search UCC records at the Secretary of State to see whether creditors have filed claims against the business's assets. The[Colorado Secretary of State](https://www.sos.state.co.us/pubs/UCC/FAQs/searching.html) says standard results include UCC financing statements, notices of liens, and federal tax liens.


A clean result has limits, because Colorado's search requires an exact name match and excludes records that lapsed more than two years ago. No result means only that nothing is on record under that name at that office.


As a practical rule, search the state where the business is organized, try known name variants, and consider other states where it operates. Compare any filings with the debts the applicant disclosed.


#### Step 10: Pull a Business Credit Report


A business credit report from a commercial credit bureau adds payment and public-record context to the checks above. Dun & Bradstreet says the[D-U-N-S Number](https://www.dnb.com/en-us/smb/duns/what-is-a-duns-number.html) from Step 2 identifies a company's business credit file.


A thin or missing file is not evidence of fraud on its own, so ask for more documentation before drawing conclusions. Use the report to confirm the business's history matches its story, and compare its listed name and address with your earlier checks.


### Red Flags That Signal a Fake or Fraudulent Company


Any one of these signs warrants a pause, and two or more together call for a deeper review before money moves:


- The legal name, EIN document, and state record do not match each other.
- The registry shows a suspended, dissolved, forfeited, or cancelled status.
- The business refuses to share its EIN, formation documents, or ownership details.
- A required license is missing, expired, or held by a different entity.
- No operating location can be confirmed through independent sources.
- The phone goes unanswered, or email comes from a free webmail account.
- The domain is newly registered even though the company claims a long history.
- Payment instructions change by email, or the company pushes for cash or an urgent wire.
- The contact creates urgency or cites a government form you cannot confirm with the agency.


### Pay Safely Until Verification Is Complete


The[California AG](https://www.oag.ca.gov/consumers/general/checking_business_bkgrd10) cautions against paying cash, writing checks, or granting bank account access for large purchases.


Prefer payment methods that you can dispute or reverse, and delay large transfers until the core checks are done.[IC3 data](https://www.ic3.gov/AnnualReport/Reports/2025_IC3Report.pdf) shows wire and ACH carried 86% of BEC transactions, so confirm any changed payment instructions by calling a number you already trust.


### Quick Business Legitimacy Checklist


Use this list for a fast first pass, then document each result:


1. Confirm the entity, status, and formation state on the Secretary of State registry.
2. Collect the EIN document and match the legal name to the state record.
3. Verify required licenses with the right state board or regulator tool.
4. Confirm the operating address and phone number through independent sources.
5. Check the email domain and the website's registration date with RDAP.
6. Search the name with "review," "complaint," and "scam," and read BBB data with care.
7. Screen the business and its owners on OFAC Sanctions List Search.
8. Collect and verify beneficial owners and the control person.
9. Search UCC filings under the exact legal name and known variants.
10. Pull a business credit report and compare it with everything above.


### Best Practices That Keep Verification Accurate


Consistent methods make each check more useful, and these habits help teams avoid the most common mistakes:


- Treat every source as one piece of evidence, because no single database proves a business is legitimate.
- Re-check registry status close to the funding date, because status is only a snapshot as of the search.
- Search exact legal names and known variants, since UCC and registry searches can miss close spellings.
- Collect identifiers and ownership from the applicant, then test them against independent records.
- Record the source, date, and result of every check so reviewers and auditors can follow the decision.
- Use IRS TIN Matching only if you are an authorized payer, and review IRS rules on how results may be used.
- Give context to missing records, since sole proprietors and private firms often have no registry or SEC entry.
- Escalate when two or more red flags appear instead of clearing them one at a time.


### How to Report a Scam Company Quickly


Speed matters most once money has moved, and the[IC3 report](https://www.ic3.gov/AnnualReport/Reports/2025_IC3Report.pdf) says that after a fraudulent transfer, "time is of the essence." Contact your financial institution immediately and ask it to request a recall of the funds.


Then file a complaint at[ic3.gov](https://www.ic3.gov/) , which the FBI urges regardless of the amount lost. In 2025, IC3's Recovery Asset Team froze about $679 million across 3,900 incidents, a 58% success rate for the cases it handled.


Report scams and bad business practices to the FTC at[ReportFraud.ftc.gov](https://reportfraud.ftc.gov/) . You can also alert your state Attorney General, your local consumer protection agency, and the licensing board for the industry involved.


### Layer Checks to Lend and Pay With Confidence


The most reliable way to verify a business is legitimate is to layer checks, because each record confirms a different fact. When those records agree, confidence rises, and when they conflict, the conflict tells you where to dig.


For lenders, the key takeaway is to build these checks into the underwriting workflow so verification happens consistently on every application. Consolidated data and automated decision rules keep reviews fast without lowering the standard of proof.


### Frequently Asked Questions


#### How Can I Verify if a Business Is Legitimate?


Confirm the business's registration and good standing with the Secretary of State, then validate its EIN and required licenses. Cross-check its address, phone, email, and website, screen it against OFAC lists, complaints, UCC liens, and credit data, and watch for red flags.


#### How Do I Verify if a Business Is Registered?


Search the Secretary of State registry in the state where the business says it was formed, using its exact legal name. Review the status, agent, and officers, and request a certificate of good standing or status if you need certified proof.


#### How Can I Check if a Company Is Legit for Free?


Several official tools are free, including SEC EDGAR, NMLS Consumer Access, and Colorado's online UCC search. Public tools such as state registry searches, FINRA BrokerCheck, OFAC Sanctions List Search, and ICANN's RDAP lookup cover most of the remaining steps.


#### What Are the Warning Signs of a Fake Company?


Common warning signs include records that do not match, an inactive registry status, missing licenses, and an unverifiable address or phone number. Pressure to pay by wire or cash, changed payment instructions, and a newly registered domain are also strong reasons to pause.


#### Is a Company Legitimate if It Has a Professional Website?


A professional website alone proves very little, because the FTC notes that anyone can put up a website under almost any name. Check the domain's registration date, then confirm the business through state records, licenses, and independent contact details.
